legend: Regina was driving Andrew to his dreaded tennis practice when he proposed to her a very interesting question. Andrew gave Regina a simple graph of N$$$N$$$ (1≤N≤2⋅105$$$1 \leq N \leq 2\cdot 10^5$$$) nodes and M$$$M$$$ (0≤M≤3⋅105$$$0 \leq M \leq 3\cdot 10^5$$$) edges, and he requested Regina to find 4$$$4$$$ distinct nodes a$$$a$$$, b$$$b$$$, c$$$c$$$, and d$$$d$$$ such that (a,b)$$$(a, b)$$$, (b,c)$$$(b, c)$$$, and (c,d)$$$(c, d)$$$ are all edges in the graph. Help her find nodes that satisfy these conditions, or output -1$$$1$$$ if no such nodes exist.
input: The first line contains two integers: N$$$N$$$ and M$$$M$$$.
The following M$$$M$$$ lines contain two integers: u$$$u$$$ and v$$$v$$$, denoting an edge between u$$$u$$$ and v$$$v$$$.
It is guaranteed that 1≤N≤2⋅105$$$1\leq N\leq2 \cdot 10^5$$$ and 0≤M≤3⋅105$$$0\leq M \leq 3 \cdot 10^5$$$.
There are no self-loops or duplicate edges in the graph.
output: If it is impossible to find four nodes that satisfy the conditions, output −1$$$-1$$$.
Otherwise, on 4$$$4$$$ separate lines, output the four nodes a$$$a$$$, b$$$b$$$, c$$$c$$$, and d$$$d$$$ with ab$$$ab$$$, bc$$$bc$$$, and cd$$$cd$$$ adjacent.
